query: Has any experimental spray-drying study embedded a mechanistic equation for atomization, droplet shrinkage, or particle formation in a data-fitted structural causal model, causal Bayesian network, or process graph, and then tested its predictions after deliberately changing a real dryer setting? Which settings and responses were tested on physical runs outside calibration? Include food and chemical applications as well as pharmaceutical spray drying.
follow_ups: Which spray-drying experiments tested a mechanistic causal model by changing a dryer setting in runs held out from model fitting?

query: Which spray-drying studies use a grey-box model, hybrid digital twin, probabilistic process model, or model-based experimental design to link operating settings, wet droplets, and dry particle properties? Look for studies that fit or constrain a physical equation with process data and then predict the response to a new physical experiment. Include papers that do not use the terms causal inference or Bayesian network.
follow_ups: Which grey-box spray-drying models predicted measured particle properties in new dryer runs after calibration?

query: In experimental engineering or manufacturing, which studies kept the same causal graph, input variables, and calibration data but compared empirical node equations with first-principles or grey-box equations? Did they compare predictions under new physical interventions, or only prediction on historical data and simulations? What improved, and under which conditions did the physical constraints fail?
follow_ups: Which manufacturing experiments compared empirical and physics-based node equations on new operating conditions while keeping the causal graph, inputs, and training data fixed?
